statement: Let $E_{ij}=\sum_{a}x_{ia}\partial_{ja}$ act on $\mathbb{C}[x_{ij}]$ for $1\le i,j\le n$. The column [determinant](c:determinant) of $E+\operatorname{diag}(n-1,\dots,0)$, with the factors taken in column order, equals $\det(x_{ij})\det(\partial_{ij})$ as [differential operators](c:differential-operator).

hypotheses.text: The operators act on the [polynomial ring](c:polynomial-ring) $\mathbb{C}[x_{ij}]$ in $n^2$ commuting variables.
Each diagonal entry $E_{ii}$ carries the shift $n-i$, and each term multiplies its factors in increasing column order.

conclusion: The column determinant equals $\det(x_{ij})\det(\partial_{ij})$ as operators.

proofs.name: Highest weight comparison
proofs.slogan: Both sides are invariant under the two actions of $GL_n$, so each acts by one scalar on every multiplicity-free piece, and the scalars agree.
proofs.scope: The identity for every $n\ge1$. The proof is an outline: the centrality of the Capelli determinant, the multiplicity-free decomposition and Cayley's identity for minors are cited.

roles.why: Commuting variables make $\det(x)$ and $\det(\partial)$ ordinary determinants and give the multiplicity-free decomposition of the [polynomial ring](c:polynomial-ring).
The shift $n-i$ makes the Capelli determinant commute with every $E_{ij}$ and gives the eigenvalue $\prod_j(\lambda_j+n-j)$.

steps.slogan: Realize the polarization operators as the generators of the left action of $GL_n$.
steps.detail: The operators $E_{ij}$ satisfy $[E_{ij},E_{kl}]=\delta_{jk}E_{il}-\delta_{il}E_{kj}$, so they give a representation of the [general linear Lie algebra](c:gl-n) $\mathfrak{gl}_n$ on $\mathbb{C}[x_{ij}]$. It differentiates the action of $GL_n$ on the rows of $X$. The action on the columns gives operators that commute with every $E_{ij}$.

steps.slogan: Show that both operators commute with the left and right actions of $GL_n$.
steps.detail: Under each action $\det(X)$ scales by $\det g$ and $\det(\partial)$ by $\det g^{-1}$, so $\det(X)\det(\partial)$ is invariant. The Capelli determinant commutes with every $E_{ij}$ by Capelli's centrality theorem, and with the column action because that action commutes with each $E_{ij}$.

steps.slogan: Split the polynomials into multiplicity-free pieces for $GL_n\times GL_n$.
steps.detail: Cauchy's decomposition gives $\mathbb{C}[x_{ij}]=\bigoplus_\lambda V_\lambda\otimes V_\lambda^{*}$ over partitions $\lambda$ with at most $n$ parts, and the summands are pairwise inequivalent [irreducible representations](c:irreducible-representation). By Schur's lemma, an invariant operator acts on each summand by one scalar.

steps.slogan: Evaluate the Capelli determinant on a highest weight vector of weight $\lambda$.
steps.detail: Let $v$ be a [highest weight](c:highest-weight) vector, so $E_{ij}v=0$ for $i<j$. In a term with $\sigma\ne\mathrm{id}$, let $k$ be the largest index with $\sigma(k)\ne k$. Then $\sigma(k)<k$, the factors to the right of $E_{\sigma(k)k}$ are diagonal and act on $v$ by scalars, and $E_{\sigma(k)k}$ kills $v$. Only $\sigma=\mathrm{id}$ survives, and it gives $\prod_j(\lambda_j+n-j)$.

steps.slogan: Evaluate $\det(X)\det(\partial)$ on the same vector by Cayley's identity.
steps.detail: The vector $\det(\partial)v$ is a multiple of the highest weight vector of weight $\lambda-(1,\dots,1)$, and Cayley's identity for minors gives the multiple $\prod_j(\lambda_j+n-j)$. Multiplying by $\det(X)$ restores $v$, so $\det(X)\det(\partial)$ acts on $v$ by the same scalar.

steps.slogan: Compare the two scalars on every summand to conclude equality.
steps.detail: Each summand is generated by its highest weight vector under $GL_n\times GL_n$, and both operators are invariant. Equal scalars on $v$ give equal scalars on the summand, so the operators agree on all polynomials. A differential operator with polynomial coefficients is determined by its action on polynomials.

concepts.c:determinant: The identity compares a column determinant with a product of ordinary determinants.
concepts.c:differential-operator: Both sides are differential operators, so equality is checked on polynomials.
concepts.c:polynomial-ring: The polynomial ring is the space on which all operators act.
concepts.c:gl-n: The operators $E_{ij}$ realize this Lie algebra and give the left symmetry.
concepts.c:irreducible-representation: Pairwise inequivalent irreducible summands make invariant operators scalar by Schur's lemma.
concepts.c:highest-weight: A highest weight vector kills every non-diagonal term of the determinant.

source.ref: R. Howe and T. Umeda, The Capelli identity, the double commutant theorem, and multiplicity-free actions, Mathematische Annalen 290 (1991), 565-619
source.note: The outline follows the representation-theoretic proof: invariance, multiplicity-free decomposition and a highest weight computation. Centrality of the Capelli determinant and Cayley's identity for minors are cited, not reproved.

statement: Take a nontrivial [S-matrix](c:s-matrix) in $3+1$ dimensions that is Poincaré invariant, has a mass gap, finitely many particle types below each mass, and analytic elastic amplitudes. Then the [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) of its connected symmetry group, which contains the Poincaré algebra, is the direct sum of the [Poincaré algebra](c:poincare-lie-algebra) and an internal algebra of Lorentz scalar charges.

hypotheses.text: The [S-matrix](c:s-matrix) is Lorentz invariant and nontrivial, and the spectrum has a mass gap.
Only finitely many particle types have mass below any given bound.
Elastic scattering amplitudes are analytic in energy and momentum transfer near the physical region.
The symmetry group is a connected Lie group containing the [Poincaré group](c:poincare-group), and its generators act on multiparticle states as sums over the particles.

conclusion: The symmetry algebra is the direct sum of the [Poincaré algebra](c:poincare-lie-algebra) and an internal [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) whose generators are Lorentz scalars commuting with translations.

proofs.name: Extra conservation laws against analyticity
proofs.slogan: Any generator beyond the Poincaré algebra would add conservation laws that restrict elastic scattering angles, which analyticity forbids.
proofs.scope: The theorem for a $3+1$ dimensional theory with the listed assumptions; the proof is an outline of the Coleman-Mandula argument. Supersymmetric extensions, which drop the assumption that charges are bosonic, are other members of the family (Haag-Lopuszanski-Sohnius).

roles.why: The generators commute with the [S-matrix](c:s-matrix), and nontrivial scattering supplies the elastic amplitude that analyticity then constrains.
Finitely many particle types give finite kernels for one-particle states and exclude a scaling generator.
Analyticity makes the elastic amplitude nonzero on an open set of angles.
A Lie group containing the [Poincaré group](c:poincare-group) with additive generators gives the tensor decomposition and the final splitting.

steps.slogan: Split the symmetry generators into Lorentz tensor operators.
steps.detail: The Poincaré algebra acts on the symmetry algebra by commutators, so the generators split into Lorentz tensors. Finiteness of particle types lets each generator act on one-particle states through a finite family of kernels in momentum space, and additivity extends the action to all multiparticle states.

steps.slogan: Turn each extra generator into a conservation law for elastic scattering.
steps.detail: A generator commutes with the S-matrix, so it gives a conserved quantity beyond the total momentum in two-particle elastic scattering. A tensor generator of rank at least two adds conditions on the final momenta that allow only special scattering angles.

steps.slogan: Contradict analyticity of the elastic amplitude.
steps.detail: Analyticity and nontrivial scattering make the elastic amplitude nonzero on an open set of angles at fixed energy. This conflicts with the angle restrictions of the previous step, so no tensor generator of higher rank than the Poincaré generators exists.

steps.slogan: Show that the remaining generators are Lorentz scalars commuting with translations.
steps.detail: Every generator outside the Poincaré algebra is now a Lorentz scalar $B$, and $[B,P^\mu]$ is a vector generator, so it equals $cP^\mu$. If $c\ne0$, the group would map a particle of mass $m$ to particles of every mass $e^{cs}m$, against finiteness of particle types. So $c=0$.

steps.slogan: Split the algebra into the Poincaré part and the internal part.
steps.detail: The scalar generators form a subalgebra that commutes with the Poincaré algebra and meets it only in zero. So the symmetry algebra is the direct sum of the Poincaré algebra and this internal algebra.

concepts.c:s-matrix: Symmetries are the transformations that commute with the S-matrix.
concepts.c:lie-algebra: The theorem splits the Lie algebra of the symmetry group into two parts.
concepts.c:poincare-lie-algebra: It is the spacetime part of the symmetry algebra in the splitting.
concepts.c:poincare-group: The symmetry group contains it and acts on generators by commutators.

source.ref: S. Coleman and J. Mandula, All possible symmetries of the S matrix, Physical Review 159 (1967), 1251-1256
source.note: Outline of the original argument; Weinberg, The Quantum Theory of Fields III, section 24.B, gives a textbook version. The finer analysis of kernels and angles is cited, not reproduced.

statement: Fix a numbering $\varphi$ of the partial [computable functions](c:computable-function) with a [Blum complexity measure](c:blum-complexity-measure) $\Phi$, and let $C^f$ be the set of $\varphi_i$ with $\Phi_i(x)\le f(x)$ for almost all $x$. For every total computable $f$, some total computable $0$-$1$ valued function is not in $C^f$.

hypotheses.text: The function $\Phi$ is a [Blum complexity measure](c:blum-complexity-measure) for $\varphi$: $\Phi_i(x)$ is defined exactly when $\varphi_i(x)$ is, and the relation $\Phi_i(x)\le y$ is decidable.
The boundary function $f$ is a total [computable function](c:computable-function).

conclusion: Some total computable $g$ with values in $\{0,1\}$ lies outside the [complexity class](c:complexity-class) $C^f$, so no class with a computable boundary holds all computable functions.

proofs.name: Diagonal cancellation
proofs.slogan: Build $g$ by flipping, input by input, the value of one cheap program, so each program for $g$ is expensive infinitely often.
proofs.scope: The whole statement, for every total computable $f$. The same $g$ also gives a computable $F\ge f$ with $C^f\subsetneq C^F$, by taking $F=\max(f,\Phi_i)$ for a program $i$ of $g$.

roles.why: The [Blum axioms](c:blum-complexity-measure) make the cheapness test decidable and make the value of a cheap program computable.
A total [computable](c:computable-function) boundary lets the test run at every input, and it is the bound that the assumed program for $g$ must meet.

steps.slogan: Decide whether a program is cheap at input $x$.
steps.detail: For $i\le x$, the test $\Phi_i(x)\le f(x)$ is decidable, because $f(x)$ is computable and the Blum measure makes the bound relation decidable. If the test succeeds, then $\varphi_i(x)$ is defined and can be computed.

steps.slogan: Define $g$ by flipping the value of the least uncancelled cheap program.
steps.detail: Define $g(x)$ by recursion on $x$. Let $i$ be the least index $\le x$ that is not cancelled at an earlier input and passes the test. If $i$ exists, put $g(x)=1$ when $\varphi_i(x)=0$ and $g(x)=0$ otherwise, and cancel $i$. If no such $i$ exists, put $g(x)=0$. The function $g$ is total, computable and $0$-$1$ valued.

steps.slogan: Show that a cheap program for $g$ is chosen at some input.
steps.detail: Suppose $g=\varphi_i$ and $\Phi_i(x)\le f(x)$ for all $x\ge x_0$. At each $x\ge\max(i,x_0)$, index $i$ passes the test, so either $i$ is chosen or a smaller index is chosen and cancelled. Only $i$ smaller indices exist, each cancelled once, so $i$ is chosen at some such $x$.

steps.slogan: Contradict $g=\varphi_i$ at the input where $i$ is chosen.
steps.detail: At that input $g(x)\ne\varphi_i(x)$ by the flip, which contradicts $g=\varphi_i$. So no program $i$ for $g$ satisfies $\Phi_i(x)\le f(x)$ for almost all $x$, and $g\notin C^f$.

concepts.c:computable-function: The boundary and the constructed function $g$ are computable functions.
concepts.c:blum-complexity-measure: Its two axioms make the diagonal construction effective.
concepts.c:complexity-class: The class $C^f$ is the set of functions that a bounded program computes.

source.note: A diagonal construction in the style of M. Blum, A machine-independent theory of the complexity of recursive functions, J. ACM 14 (1967), 322-336; it proves the lead statement of the compression theorem.

statement: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a full, replete [reflective subcategory](c:reflective-subcategory) of a symmetric [closed monoidal category](c:closed-monoidal-category) $\mathcal{D}$, with reflector $L$ and unit $u$. These are equivalent: (a) $[d,c]\in\mathcal{C}$ for all $d\in\mathcal{D}$, $c\in\mathcal{C}$; (b) $L(u_d\otimes 1_{d'})$ is invertible for all $d,d'$; (c) $L(u_d\otimes u_{d'})$ is invertible for all $d,d'$.

hypotheses.text: The category $\mathcal{D}$ is symmetric [closed monoidal](c:closed-monoidal-category), with internal hom $[d,-]$ right adjoint to $-\otimes d$.
The subcategory $\mathcal{C}$ is full, replete and [reflective](c:reflective-subcategory) in $\mathcal{D}$, with unit $u_d\colon d\to Ld$.

conclusion: Conditions (a), (b) and (c) are equivalent; in particular $\mathcal{C}$ is closed under the [internal hom](c:internal-hom) of $\mathcal{D}$ exactly when $L$ inverts $u_d\otimes 1_{d'}$.

proofs.name: Yoneda transpose
proofs.slogan: Transpose maps along the tensor-hom and reflection adjunctions, then detect membership in $\mathcal{C}$ and invertibility by Yoneda.
proofs.scope: The whole equivalence of (a), (b) and (c); (a) and (b) are shown for each fixed $d'$. We write $Ld$ for the object $L d$ viewed in $\mathcal{D}$.

roles.why: The tensor-hom adjunction transposes maps, and the symmetry swaps the two tensor factors in step 4.
The reflection gives bijections out of $L$-images and the unique extension property of units.

steps.slogan: Transpose maps out of tensor products along both adjunctions.
steps.detail: For $c\in\mathcal{C}$ there are bijections, natural in $d$ and given by the [adjoint functor](c:adjoint-functor) pairs: $\mathcal{D}(d,[d',c])\cong\mathcal{D}(d\otimes d',c)\cong\mathcal{C}(L(d\otimes d'),c)$. Under them, precomposition with $u_d$ on the left matches precomposition with $L(u_d\otimes 1_{d'})$ on the right.

steps.slogan: Characterize objects of $\mathcal{C}$ by unique extension along units.
steps.detail: An object $e$ lies in $\mathcal{C}$ exactly when every map $d\to e$ factors uniquely through $u_d$. If $e\in\mathcal{C}$, this is the universal property of $u_d$. Conversely, extend $1_e$ along $u_e$ to $r$; then $u_er$ and $1_{Le}$ both extend $u_e$, so $u_er=1$ and $u_e$ is invertible.

steps.slogan: Show that (a) and (b) are equivalent for each $d'$ by Yoneda.
steps.detail: By the two previous steps, $[d',c]\in\mathcal{C}$ for all $c$ exactly when precomposition with $L(u_d\otimes1_{d'})$ is bijective on $\mathcal{C}(-,c)$ for all $c$ and $d$. By the Yoneda lemma in $\mathcal{C}$, this holds exactly when $L(u_d\otimes1_{d'})$ is invertible.

steps.slogan: Show that (b) and (c) are equivalent by factoring $u_d\otimes u_{d'}$.
steps.detail: We have $u_d\otimes u_{d'}=(1_{Ld}\otimes u_{d'})(u_d\otimes1_{d'})$, and symmetry turns (b) into invertibility of $L(1\otimes u_{d'})$, so (b) gives (c). For (c) to (b): $u_{Ld}$ is invertible, so (c) at $Ld$ makes $L(1_{Ld}\otimes u_{d'})$ invertible, and then $L(u_d\otimes1_{d'})$ is a quotient of invertible maps.

steps.slogan: Join the two equivalences over all objects.
steps.detail: Step 3 gives (a) if and only if (b), by quantifying over $d'$. Step 4 gives (b) if and only if (c). Hence (a), (b) and (c) are equivalent.

concepts.c:closed-monoidal-category: Its tensor-hom adjunction supplies the internal hom and transposition of maps.
concepts.c:reflective-subcategory: The reflector $L$ and its unit are the data that the conditions test.
concepts.c:internal-hom: Condition (a) says that the subcategory is closed under this operation.
concepts.c:adjoint-functor: Transposing along adjunctions turns maps into $[d',c]$ into maps out of $L$-images.

source.note: The Yoneda argument for the theorem of B. Day, A reflection theorem for closed categories, J. Pure Appl. Algebra 2 (1972), 1-11.

statement: Let $A$ be an [associative algebra](c:associative-algebra) over a field. Then the Hochschild cochain complex $C^\bullet(A,A)$ is naturally an [algebra over an operad](c:algebra-over-an-operad) quasi-isomorphic to the chains of the [little disks operad](c:little-disks-operad) $D_2$. So [Hochschild cohomology](c:hochschild-cohomology) is a [Gerstenhaber algebra](c:gerstenhaber-algebra) for the cup product and the bracket.

hypotheses.text: The algebra $A$ is an [associative algebra](c:associative-algebra) over a field $k$.

conclusion: The complex $C^\bullet(A,A)$ is an algebra over a chain operad quasi-isomorphic to $C_*(D_2)$, and the induced structure on $HH^\bullet(A,A)$ is the Gerstenhaber structure.

proofs.name: Cosimplicial operad with multiplication
proofs.slogan: View the cochains as the totalization of a cosimplicial object from an operad with multiplication, act on it by a combinatorial dg operad, and compare that operad with little disks.
proofs.scope: Deligne's question as asked, for associative algebras over a field; the proof is an outline of the McClure-Smith solution, and other proofs (Kontsevich-Soibelman, Tamarkin, Voronov) exist. Framed and BV variants for Frobenius or Calabi-Yau algebras are other members of the family and are not proved here.

roles.why: The multiplication of the [associative algebra](c:associative-algebra) gives the operad with multiplication whose totalization is the Hochschild complex.

steps.slogan: Present the cochains through the endomorphism operad of $A$.
steps.detail: The multiplication gives a map from the associative [operad](c:operad) to the endomorphism operad $\mathrm{End}_A$, so $\mathrm{End}_A$ is an operad with multiplication. The spaces $\mathrm{Hom}(A^{\otimes n},A)$ form a cosimplicial object whose totalization is $C^\bullet(A,A)$.

steps.slogan: Write the cup product and the brace operations on the totalization.
steps.detail: The cosimplicial structure gives explicit operations on $C^\bullet(A,A)$: the cup product and the brace operations $f\{g_1,\dots,g_k\}$. The circle product $f\{g\}$ gives the Gerstenhaber bracket, and the braces satisfy the brace operad relations of Gerstenhaber and Voronov.

steps.slogan: Extend these operations to an action of a combinatorial dg operad.
steps.detail: McClure and Smith define a dg operad whose operations are indexed by combinatorial data on finite sets (sequences, equivalently surjections). They give its action on the totalization by explicit formulas in the cosimplicial structure, and the operations of the previous step are its low-arity generators.

steps.slogan: Compare this combinatorial operad with the little disks operad.
steps.detail: This dg operad is quasi-isomorphic to the singular chains of the little 2-cubes operad, which is equivalent to $D_2$ (McClure and Smith). So $C^\bullet(A,A)$ is an algebra over a dg operad quasi-isomorphic to $C_*(D_2)$.

steps.slogan: Pass to cohomology to read off the Gerstenhaber structure.
steps.detail: The homology of the little 2-disks operad is the Gerstenhaber operad. So the induced product and bracket on $HH^\bullet(A,A)$ satisfy the Gerstenhaber relations, and they are the cup product and bracket of the second step.

concepts.c:associative-algebra: The algebra $A$ supplies the multiplication and the cochain complex.
concepts.c:algebra-over-an-operad: The theorem says that the cochain complex is such an algebra.
concepts.c:little-disks-operad: Its chains are the model operad that acts on the cochains.
concepts.c:hochschild-cohomology: It is the cohomology of the cochain complex that carries the action.
concepts.c:gerstenhaber-algebra: The homology of the little 2-disks operad gives this structure on cohomology.
concepts.c:operad: The endomorphism operad with multiplication is the source of the cosimplicial object.

source.ref: J. E. McClure and J. H. Smith, A solution of Deligne's Hochschild cohomology conjecture, in Recent Progress in Homotopy Theory (Baltimore, MD, 2000), Contemporary Mathematics 293, American Mathematical Society, 2002, 153-193
source.note: The steps outline the McClure-Smith construction; the formulas of the operad action and the operad comparison are cited.

statement: Every [combinatorial model category](c:combinatorial-model-category) $M$ is [Quillen equivalent](c:quillen-equivalence) to a left [Bousfield localization](c:bousfield-localization) $L_S\,\mathrm{sPre}(C)$ of the projective model structure on [simplicial presheaves](c:simplicial-presheaf) on a small category $C$, localized at a set $S$ of maps.

hypotheses.text: The model category $M$ is combinatorial: cofibrantly generated and [locally presentable](c:locally-presentable-category).

conclusion: There are a small category $C$, a set $S$ of maps of simplicial presheaves on $C$, and a Quillen equivalence between $M$ and $L_S\,\mathrm{sPre}(C)$.

proofs.name: Generators and relations
proofs.slogan: Choose generators in $M$, map the simplicial presheaves on them into $M$, and localize at the relations among them until the map is an equivalence.
proofs.scope: Dugger's theorem for every combinatorial model category; the proof is an outline of Dugger's argument, and the left properness of the result is not discussed.

roles.why: Local presentability gives a small set of generators, and cofibrant generation gives the localization and the simplicial replacement.

steps.slogan: Replace $M$ by a Quillen equivalent simplicial combinatorial model category.
steps.detail: Dugger shows that a combinatorial model category is Quillen equivalent to a simplicial one, so that homotopy function complexes become simplicial mapping spaces. The replacement is again combinatorial, so assume that $M$ is simplicial.

steps.slogan: Choose a small set of $\lambda$-presentable cofibrant generators.
steps.detail: Pick a regular cardinal $\lambda$ for which $M$ is locally $\lambda$-presentable. Let $C$ be a small full subcategory of cofibrant $\lambda$-presentable objects that generates $M$ under $\lambda$-filtered homotopy colimits.

steps.slogan: Build a Quillen pair from the universal property of simplicial presheaves.
steps.detail: The inclusion $C\to M$ extends to a left Quillen functor $\mathrm{sPre}(C)\to M$ whose right adjoint sends $a$ to the presheaf $c\mapsto\mathrm{Map}(c,a)$. This is the universal property of simplicial presheaves from Dugger's Universal homotopy theories.

steps.slogan: Choose a set $S$ of relations and localize at it.
steps.detail: Let $S$ be a set of maps of $\mathrm{sPre}(C)$ that records the homotopy colimit relations among the objects of $C$ valid in $M$. The left [Bousfield localization](c:bousfield-localization) $L_S$ exists since $\mathrm{sPre}(C)$ is left proper and combinatorial, and the Quillen pair descends to $L_S$.

steps.slogan: Check that the localized Quillen pair is a Quillen equivalence.
steps.detail: The right adjoint preserves $\lambda$-filtered homotopy colimits and detects weak equivalences between fibrant objects through the maps $\mathrm{Map}(c,-)$ for $c\in C$. Since $C$ generates $M$ under such homotopy colimits, the derived unit and counit are equivalences.

concepts.c:combinatorial-model-category: These are the model categories that the theorem presents by generators.
concepts.c:quillen-equivalence: The conclusion is that the localized pair is such an equivalence.
concepts.c:bousfield-localization: Localizing at the relations $S$ cuts the presheaf category down to $M$.
concepts.c:simplicial-presheaf: These are the free model category on the generators.
concepts.c:locally-presentable-category: Local presentability gives a small generating set of presentable objects.

source.ref: D. Dugger, Combinatorial model categories have presentations, Advances in Mathematics 164 (2001), 177-201
source.note: The steps outline Dugger's argument; the simplicial replacement, the choice of $S$ and the equivalence check are cited.

statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $M$ and $N$ be $R$-modules, and let $m_1,\dots,m_k$ generate $M$. For $n_1,\dots,n_k\in N$, $\sum_i m_i\otimes n_i=0$ in the [tensor product](c:tensor-product) $M\otimes_R N$ if and only if there are $y_j\in N$ and $a_{ij}\in R$ with $n_i=\sum_j a_{ij}y_j$ and the [linear relations](c:linear-relation) $\sum_i a_{ij}m_i=0$ for all $j$.

hypotheses.text: The ring $R$ is commutative and $M$, $N$ are $R$-[modules](c:module).
The families $(m_i)$ in $M$ and $(n_i)$ in $N$ are finite, indexed by $i=1,\dots,k$.
The elements $m_1,\dots,m_k$ generate $M$.

conclusion: The sum $\sum_i m_i\otimes n_i$ vanishes exactly when the data $a_{ij}$ and $y_j$ exist.

formal.difference: The declaration proves only that trivial vanishing implies vanishing, which needs no generation hypothesis. The converse is the separate declaration TensorProduct.vanishesTrivially_of_sum_tmul_eq_zero.

proofs.name: Right exactness of the tensor product
proofs.slogan: One direction moves scalars across the tensor sign, and the other lifts the vanishing element through a presentation of $M$ by right exactness.
proofs.scope: The whole equivalence. The easy direction needs no generation hypothesis; the converse uses that the $m_i$ generate $M$.

roles.why: Commutativity lets scalars move across the tensor sign and makes the tensor product an $R$-module.
Finiteness makes the sums finite and gives the free module $R^k$.
Generation makes the map $G\colon R^k\to M$ surjective, which right exactness needs.

steps.slogan: Substitute $n_i=\sum_j a_{ij}y_j$ and swap the finite sums.
steps.detail: If the relations hold, bilinearity gives $\sum_i m_i\otimes n_i=\sum_i\sum_j m_i\otimes a_{ij}y_j$. The scalar $a_{ij}$ moves across the tensor sign, so this equals $\sum_j(\sum_i a_{ij}m_i)\otimes y_j$. Each inner sum is zero and $0\otimes y=0$, so the whole sum vanishes.

steps.slogan: Present $M$ as a quotient of the [free module](c:free-module) $R^k$.
steps.detail: Let $G\colon R^k\to M$ send the basis vector $e_i$ to $m_i$. It is surjective because the $m_i$ generate $M$. Let $K=\ker G$.

steps.slogan: Place $\sum_i e_i\otimes n_i$ in the kernel of $G\otimes 1_N$.
steps.detail: The element $\epsilon=\sum_i e_i\otimes n_i\in R^k\otimes N$ maps to $\sum_i m_i\otimes n_i$ under $G\otimes 1_N$. Assume that this image is zero. Then $\epsilon$ lies in the kernel of $G\otimes1_N$.

steps.slogan: Lift $\epsilon$ to $K\otimes N$ by right exactness.
steps.detail: The sequence $K\otimes N\to R^k\otimes N\to M\otimes N\to0$ is an [exact sequence](c:exact-sequence), because the tensor product is right exact. So $\epsilon$ is the image of some $\sum_j\kappa_j\otimes y_j$ with $\kappa_j\in K$ and $y_j\in N$.

steps.slogan: Read off the coefficients $a_{ij}$ from the elements $\kappa_j$.
steps.detail: Let $a_{ij}$ be the $e_i$-coordinate of $\kappa_j$. Comparing $e_i$-components in $R^k\otimes N\cong N^k$ gives $n_i=\sum_j a_{ij}y_j$. Since $\kappa_j\in\ker G$, we get $\sum_i a_{ij}m_i=G(\kappa_j)=0$.

steps.slogan: Combine both directions into the criterion.
steps.detail: The first step proves that trivial vanishing implies vanishing, with no generation hypothesis. The steps from the presentation to the coefficients prove the converse when the $m_i$ generate $M$. Together they give the equivalence.

concepts.c:tensor-product: The sum lives in $M\otimes_R N$, and vanishing there is the question.
concepts.c:linear-relation: The coefficients $a_{ij}$ give relations among the $m_i$ that cause vanishing.
concepts.c:module: The tensor product and the scalars $a_{ij}$ live in module language.
concepts.c:free-module: The module $R^k$ presents $M$ and holds the element $\epsilon$.
concepts.c:exact-sequence: Right exactness gives exactness at $R^k\otimes N$, which lifts $\epsilon$.

source.note: mathlib moves scalars across the tensor sign and swaps the sums (tmul_sum, tmul_smul, Finset.sum_comm). The converse follows TensorProduct.vanishesTrivially_of_sum_tmul_eq_zero, which uses rTensor_exact.

statement: Let $\gamma\colon\mathbb{R}/L\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{R}^3$ be a [closed curve](c:closed-curve) of class $C^2$ parametrized by arclength. Then its [total curvature](c:total-curvature) is at least $2\pi$: $\int_0^L\kappa\,ds\ge2\pi$, where $\kappa=|\gamma''|$.

hypotheses.text: The curve is a [closed curve](c:closed-curve): $\gamma$ is $L$-periodic.
The curve is $C^2$ with $|\gamma'|=1$, so that the [curvature](c:curvature) $\kappa=|\gamma''|$ is defined.

conclusion: The total curvature $\int_0^L\kappa\,ds$ is at least $2\pi$.

proofs.name: Counting critical points of height functions
proofs.slogan: The total curvature is the length of the tangent indicatrix, which is an average count of critical points of height functions, and each count is at least two.
proofs.scope: The inequality for every closed $C^2$ curve; equality cases are not treated. A curve with a point of zero curvature is covered, since the length of the indicatrix is $\int|T'|\,ds$ in all cases.

roles.why: Periodicity gives every height function a maximum and a minimum on the circle.
Smoothness makes the tangent indicatrix a $C^1$ curve with speed equal to the [curvature](c:curvature).

steps.slogan: Replace the curve by its unit tangent indicatrix on the sphere.
steps.detail: Let $T=\gamma'\colon\mathbb{R}/L\mathbb{Z}\to S^2$. Then $|T'|=|\gamma''|=\kappa$, so $\int_0^L\kappa\,ds$ is the length of the closed curve $T$ on the [unit sphere](c:unit-sphere).

steps.slogan: Write the length of $T$ as an average count of great-circle crossings.
steps.detail: For $v\in S^2$ let $N(v)$ be the number of $s$ with $\langle T(s),v\rangle=0$. Parametrize the pairs $(s,v)$ with $v\perp T(s)$ by $s$ and an angle $\varphi$ along the great circle $T(s)^\perp$. The area formula gives $\int_{S^2}N\,dA=\int_0^L\int_0^{2\pi}|T'(s)||\cos\varphi|\,d\varphi\,ds=4\int_0^L\kappa\,ds$.

steps.slogan: Show that every height function has at least two critical points.
steps.detail: For fixed $v$, the function $h(s)=\langle\gamma(s),v\rangle$ is periodic and $C^1$, so it has a maximum and a minimum. At these points $h'=\langle T,v\rangle=0$. If $h$ is constant, every $s$ is a zero. Otherwise the two extrema are distinct. So $N(v)\ge2$ for every $v$.

steps.slogan: Integrate the bound over the sphere.
steps.detail: The previous two steps give $4\int_0^L\kappa\,ds=\int_{S^2}N\,dA\ge2\cdot4\pi$, because $S^2$ has area $4\pi$. Hence $\int_0^L\kappa\,ds\ge2\pi$.

concepts.c:closed-curve: Closedness gives each height function a maximum and a minimum.
concepts.c:total-curvature: It is the quantity bounded below, and equals the length of the indicatrix.
concepts.c:curvature: The curvature is the speed of the tangent indicatrix.
concepts.c:unit-sphere: The tangent indicatrix lives there, and its length is averaged over directions.

source.note: The counting proof of J. Milnor, On the total curvature of knots, Annals of Mathematics 52 (1950), 248-257, with the crossing formula derived by the area formula.

statement: A [simple closed curve](c:simple-closed-curve) of class $C^2$ in the plane that is not a circle has at least four vertices: its [curvature](c:curvature) has at least two local maxima and at least two local minima.

hypotheses.text: The curve is a [simple closed curve](c:simple-closed-curve) in the plane.
The curve is $C^2$ and regular, so its [curvature](c:curvature) is a continuous function of arclength.

conclusion: The curvature has at least two local maxima and two local minima.

proofs.name: Circumscribed circle
proofs.slogan: Compare the curve with the smallest circle that contains it: curvature is high at the contact points and low between them.
proofs.scope: Curves that are not circles; a circle has constant curvature and every point is a vertex. The proof is an outline of Osserman's argument, which shows that $n$ contact components give at least $2n$ vertices.

roles.why: Simplicity orders the contact points along the curve and powers the comparison lemma between consecutive contacts.
A continuous [curvature](c:curvature) function lets us compare it with the constant $K$ and find interior extrema.

steps.slogan: Take the smallest circle whose disk contains the curve.
steps.detail: Let $\Gamma$ be this circle, of radius $R$, and put $K=1/R$. If the curve contains an arc of $\Gamma$, the curvature is constant on that arc and the curve has infinitely many vertices. Assume otherwise.

steps.slogan: Show that the curve touches $\Gamma$ in at least two points.
steps.detail: If all contact points lay in an open half of $\Gamma$, one could move and shrink the circle. So the contact points do not lie in an open semicircle. There are at least two of them, and consecutive ones are at most a half circle apart.

steps.slogan: Compare the curvature with $K$ at each contact point.
steps.detail: At a contact point the curve lies inside the disk and is tangent to $\Gamma$. If its [curvature](c:curvature) were below $K$ there, the curve would leave the disk. So $\kappa\ge K$ at every contact point.

steps.slogan: Find a point with curvature below $K$ between consecutive contacts.
steps.detail: Osserman's lemma gives, on each arc between two consecutive contact points, a point where $\kappa<K$. The proof compares that arc with $\Gamma$ and uses that the curve is simple.

steps.slogan: Count the alternating maxima and minima around the curve.
steps.detail: With $n\ge2$ contact points, the curve has $n$ arcs that each contain a point with $\kappa<K$, separated by contact points with $\kappa\ge K$. The minimum of $\kappa$ on each arc is a local minimum. Between two consecutive minima, the maximum is at least $K$ and is a local maximum. This gives $2n\ge4$ vertices.

concepts.c:simple-closed-curve: Simplicity keeps the arcs between contacts from crossing each other.
concepts.c:curvature: The theorem counts local extrema of the curvature against the constant $K$.

source.ref: R. Osserman, The four-or-more vertex theorem, American Mathematical Monthly 92 (1985), 332-337
source.note: The outline follows Osserman's circumscribed circle proof; the lemma that curvature drops below $K$ between consecutive contacts is cited, not reproved.

statement: Let $H=H_0+gV$ be a [Hamiltonian](c:hamiltonian) and $\Phi_0$ a normalized eigenvector of $H_0$ with $H_0\Phi_0=E_0\Phi_0$. Let $\Psi_\varepsilon$ be the normalized state $U_\varepsilon(0,-\infty)\Phi_0$ obtained by switching on $gV$ with the factor $e^{-\varepsilon|t|}$. If $\Psi_\varepsilon$ has a limit $\Psi$ as $\varepsilon\to0^+$ in every order of $g$, then $\Psi$ is an [eigenvector](c:eigenvector) of $H$.

hypotheses.text: The state $\Phi_0$ is a normalized [eigenvector](c:eigenvector) of $H_0$ with eigenvalue $E_0$.
The coupling is switched on as $g\,e^{-\varepsilon|t|}$ with $\varepsilon>0$, and all quantities are formal power series in $g$.
The normalized state $\Psi_\varepsilon=U_\varepsilon(0,-\infty)\Phi_0/\langle\Phi_0|U_\varepsilon(0,-\infty)\Phi_0\rangle$ has a limit as $\varepsilon\to0^+$ in each order of $g$.

conclusion: The limit state $\Psi$ satisfies $H\Psi=(E_0+\Delta E)\Psi$ with $\Delta E=\langle\Phi_0|gV|\Psi\rangle$.

proofs.name: Scaling of the switching factor
proofs.slogan: Shifting time rescales the coupling, which turns the Schrödinger equation into an eigenvalue equation up to a term of order $\varepsilon$.
proofs.scope: The theorem as a statement about formal power series in $g$, for any eigenvector $\Phi_0$ of $H_0$, degenerate or not. Convergence of the series and the existence of the limit are assumed, as in the theorem.

roles.why: The identity $e^{-iH_0\tau}\Phi_0=e^{-iE_0\tau}\Phi_0$ and $\langle\Phi_0|(H_0-E_0)=0$ remove $H_0$ from the equation.
The exponential switching factor makes a time shift equal to a rescaling of $g$.
Existence of the limit in each order makes the $\varepsilon g\,\partial_g$ term vanish.

steps.slogan: Shift time by $\tau\le0$ to rescale the coupling.
steps.detail: In the interaction picture, for $\tau\le0$, substituting $t'=t+\tau$ in the time-ordered exponential gives $U_\varepsilon(\tau,-\infty;g)=e^{iH_0\tau}U_\varepsilon(0,-\infty;g e^{\varepsilon\tau})e^{-iH_0\tau}$.

steps.slogan: Differentiate the scaling identity at $\tau=0$ on the state $\Phi_0$.
steps.detail: Put $\tilde\Psi=U_\varepsilon(0,-\infty)\Phi_0$. The left side has derivative $-igV\tilde\Psi$, and the right side has derivative $i(H_0-E_0)\tilde\Psi+\varepsilon g\,\partial_g\tilde\Psi$. Hence $(H-E_0)\tilde\Psi=i\varepsilon g\,\partial_g\tilde\Psi$.

steps.slogan: Divide by the normalization $N=\langle\Phi_0|\tilde\Psi\rangle$.
steps.detail: Write $\Psi_\varepsilon=\tilde\Psi/N$. The product rule gives $\partial_g\tilde\Psi=N\partial_g\Psi_\varepsilon+\Psi_\varepsilon\partial_gN$. Dividing the equation of the previous step by $N$, we obtain $(H-E_0)\Psi_\varepsilon=i\varepsilon g\,\partial_g\Psi_\varepsilon+i\varepsilon g(\partial_g\ln N)\Psi_\varepsilon$.

steps.slogan: Pair with $\langle\Phi_0|$ to identify the energy shift.
steps.detail: Take the inner product of the previous equation with $\Phi_0$. Since $\langle\Phi_0|(H_0-E_0)=0$ and $\langle\Phi_0|\Psi_\varepsilon\rangle=1$ for all $g$, the left side is $\langle\Phi_0|gV|\Psi_\varepsilon\rangle$ and $\langle\Phi_0|\partial_g\Psi_\varepsilon\rangle=0$. Hence $\langle\Phi_0|gV|\Psi_\varepsilon\rangle=i\varepsilon g\,\partial_g\ln N$.

steps.slogan: Let $\varepsilon$ go to zero order by order in $g$.
steps.detail: The coefficient of $g^n$ in $\varepsilon g\,\partial_g\Psi_\varepsilon$ is $n\varepsilon\Psi_{\varepsilon,n}$, which tends to zero because $\Psi_{\varepsilon,n}$ has a limit. The other term tends to $\Delta E\,\Psi$ with $\Delta E=\langle\Phi_0|gV|\Psi\rangle$. So $(H-E_0-\Delta E)\Psi=0$.

concepts.c:hamiltonian: The full operator $H=H_0+gV$ is the one whose eigenvector we obtain.
concepts.c:eigenvector: The free state is one, and the limit state is shown to be one of $H$.

source.note: The standard argument of M. Gell-Mann and F. Low, Bound states in quantum field theory, Physical Review 84 (1951), 350-354, as given in many-body textbooks.

statement: Let $\mu_n$ and $\mu$ be [probability measures](c:probability-measure) on $\mathbb{R}$ with [characteristic functions](c:characteristic-function) $\varphi_n$ and $\varphi$. If $\varphi_n(t)\to\varphi(t)$ for almost every $t$, then $\mu_n\to\mu$ [weakly](c:weak-convergence).

hypotheses.text: The functions $\varphi_n$ and $\varphi$ are the [characteristic functions](c:characteristic-function) of probability measures $\mu_n$ and $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$.
The convergence $\varphi_n(t)\to\varphi(t)$ holds for Lebesgue almost every $t\in\mathbb{R}$.

proofs.name: Tightness and subsequences
proofs.slogan: Show that the measures are tight, so subsequences converge weakly, and identify every limit with $\mu$ through its characteristic function.
proofs.scope: Measures on the real line; the same proof works on $\mathbb{R}^d$ with a $d$-dimensional truncation inequality. Lévy's continuity theorem assumes convergence at every point instead of almost every point.

roles.why: The form of [characteristic functions](c:characteristic-function) gives the truncation inequality, continuity at $0$ with $\varphi(0)=1$, and the uniqueness of the limit.
Almost everywhere convergence is enough for dominated convergence of the averages and for equality of continuous limits.

steps.slogan: Bound the mass far out by an average of $1-\varphi_n$.
steps.detail: For $u>0$, $\int_{-u}^{u}(1-e^{itx})\,dt=2u(1-\sin(ux)/(ux))$, which is at least $0$ for all $x$ and at least $u$ when $|x|\ge2/u$. Integrating against $\mu_n$ and using Fubini gives $\mu_n(|x|\ge2/u)\le\frac1u\int_{-u}^{u}(1-\varphi_n(t))\,dt$.

steps.slogan: Show that the sequence is [tight](c:tightness).
steps.detail: Fix $\epsilon>0$. Since $\varphi$ is continuous with $\varphi(0)=1$, choose $u$ with $\frac1u\int_{-u}^{u}(1-\varphi)\,dt<\epsilon/2$. Because $|1-\varphi_n|\le2$ and $\varphi_n\to\varphi$ almost everywhere, dominated convergence gives $\frac1u\int(1-\varphi_n)\to\frac1u\int(1-\varphi)$. So $\mu_n(|x|\ge2/u)<\epsilon$ for large $n$, and finitely many measures are tight on their own.

steps.slogan: Extract a weakly convergent subsequence from any subsequence.
steps.detail: A tight sequence of probability measures is relatively compact for weak convergence. So every subsequence of $(\mu_n)$ has a further subsequence $\mu_{n_k}$ that converges weakly to a probability measure $\nu$.

steps.slogan: Identify the limit measure $\nu$ with $\mu$.
steps.detail:
Weak convergence gives $\varphi_{n_k}(t)	o\varphi_
u(t)$ for every $t$, because $e^{itx}$ is bounded and continuous. Also $\varphi_{n_k}	o\varphi$ almost everywhere, so $\varphi_
u=\varphi$ almost everywhere. Both functions are continuous, so they agree everywhere, and the uniqueness theorem gives $
u=\mu$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the whole sequence converges weakly to $\mu$.
steps.detail: Every subsequence of $(\mu_n)$ has a further subsequence with limit $\mu$. Suppose $\mu_n\not\to\mu$. Then some bounded continuous $f$, some $\delta>0$ and a subsequence satisfy $|\int f\,d\mu_n-\int f\,d\mu|\ge\delta$, which contradicts the previous step. So $\mu_n\to\mu$.

concepts.c:probability-measure: The theorem compares sequences of probability measures on the real line.
concepts.c:characteristic-function: It determines the measure and bounds the mass far out.
concepts.c:weak-convergence: It is the mode of convergence to prove, and subsequential limits are taken in it.
concepts.c:tightness: Tightness gives weakly convergent subsequences by Prokhorov's theorem.

source.note: The truncation and subsequence argument used in textbook proofs of Lévy's continuity theorem (for example Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples), with dominated convergence replacing pointwise convergence.

statement: For a [ring](c:ring) $R$, the [global dimension](c:global-dimension) of $R$, the supremum of the [projective dimensions](c:projective-dimension) of all left modules, equals the supremum of $\mathrm{pd}(R/I)$ over left ideals $I$. It also equals the supremum of the injective dimensions of all left modules.

hypotheses.text: The ring $R$ has an identity, and modules are left $R$-modules.

conclusion: The three suprema, over all modules for projective dimension, over all modules for injective dimension, and over cyclic modules $R/I$, are equal in $\{0,1,2,\dots,\infty\}$.

proofs.name: Baer criterion and dimension shifting
proofs.slogan: Bound the injective dimension of every module by the cyclic projective dimensions through Baer's criterion, then pass back to projective dimension through Ext.
proofs.scope: Rings with identity and left modules; the case of an infinite supremum is trivial, since the global dimension is at least the cyclic supremum. The case $d=0$ gives the semisimple rings.

roles.why: The ring supplies the left ideals $I$ and the cyclic modules $R/I$ that Baer's criterion tests.

steps.slogan: Bound the cyclic supremum by the global dimension.
steps.detail: Let $a$ be the [global dimension](c:global-dimension) and $c=\sup_I\mathrm{pd}(R/I)$. Each $R/I$ is a module, so $c\le a$. If $c=\infty$ then $a=\infty$ and all three suprema agree, so assume $c\le d<\infty$ from now on.

steps.slogan: Shift dimension along an injective resolution of an arbitrary module $N$.
steps.detail: Take an [injective resolution](c:has-injective-resolution) $0\to N\to E^0\to\cdots\to E^{d-1}\to C\to0$. The long exact Ext sequences give $\mathrm{Ext}^1(R/I,C)\cong\mathrm{Ext}^{d+1}(R/I,N)$ for every left ideal $I$.

steps.slogan: Kill the Ext group by the projective dimension bound.
steps.detail: Because $\mathrm{pd}(R/I)\le d$, the group $\mathrm{Ext}^{d+1}(R/I,N)$ is zero. So $\mathrm{Ext}^1(R/I,C)=0$ for every left ideal $I$.

steps.slogan: Apply Baer's criterion to see that $C$ is injective.
steps.detail: The sequence $0\to I\to R\to R/I\to0$ gives $\mathrm{Hom}(R,C)\to\mathrm{Hom}(I,C)\to\mathrm{Ext}^1(R/I,C)=0$. So every map $I\to C$ extends to $R$, and Baer's criterion makes $C$ [injective](c:injective). Hence $\mathrm{id}\,N\le d$ for every $N$.

steps.slogan: Turn the bound on injective dimension into a bound on projective dimension.
steps.detail: The bound $\mathrm{id}\,N\le d$ for all $N$ says that $\mathrm{Ext}^{d+1}(M,N)=0$ for all $M,N$. This is equivalent to $\mathrm{pd}\,M\le d$ for all $M$. So $a\le d$, which with $c\le a$ gives $a=c$, and the same vanishing gives $\sup\mathrm{id}=a$.

concepts.c:ring: The ring and its left ideals give the cyclic modules in the statement.
concepts.c:global-dimension: It is the supremum of projective dimensions that the theorem computes.
concepts.c:projective-dimension: Its bound on cyclic modules kills the Ext group in degree $d+1$.
concepts.c:has-injective-resolution: The cosyzygy $C$ comes from an injective resolution of $N$.
concepts.c:injective: Baer's criterion shows that the cosyzygy is injective.

source.note: Auslander's theorem, proved by Baer's criterion and dimension shifting as in Weibel, An Introduction to Homological Algebra, section 4.1.

statement: In the covariantly quantized open bosonic string in $D=26$ with intercept $1$, take the [Fock space](c:fock-space) of $26$ free bosons at nonzero momentum $k$. The physical states, those with $L_n\psi=0$ for $n>0$ and $L_0\psi=\psi$ for the [Virasoro](c:virasoro-algebra) generators, have a positive semidefinite norm. Modulo null states they are isomorphic to the Fock space of the $24$ transverse oscillators.

hypotheses.text: The target dimension is $D=26$ and the intercept is $1$.
The momentum $k$ of the states is nonzero.
The state space is the [Fock space](c:fock-space) of $D$ free bosons with Lorentzian signature, so timelike oscillators have negative norm.

conclusion: The norm is positive semidefinite on the physical states, and the physical states modulo null states form the transverse oscillator Fock space.

proofs.name: Transverse DDF states
proofs.slogan: Build the transverse physical states with DDF operators, and show that every physical state is such a state plus a null spurious state.
proofs.scope: The open string in the old covariant formalism at $D=26$ and intercept $1$. The proof is an outline of the original argument; BRST proofs reach the same statement, and $D<26$ and the superstring are other members of the family.

roles.why: The values $D=26$ and intercept $1$ make the Kac determinant argument leave only DDF states and null states.
A nonzero momentum allows a null vector $q$ with $q\cdot k=1$ for the DDF operators.
The Lorentzian [Fock space](c:fock-space) is where the negative-norm oscillators appear and must be removed.

steps.slogan: Fix a null direction and split the oscillators into transverse and longitudinal ones.
steps.detail: Since $k\ne0$, choose a null vector $q$ with $q\cdot k=1$ after rescaling. The $26$ oscillator families split into $24$ transverse families and two longitudinal families along $q$ and its conjugate null direction.

steps.slogan: Build transverse physical states from the DDF operators.
steps.detail: The operators $A^i_n=\oint\partial X^i\,e^{inq\cdot X}$ for $i=1,\dots,24$ commute with the [Virasoro](c:virasoro-algebra) generators and obey the oscillator algebra. Their Fock states over the base state are physical, with the positive norm of $24$ free oscillators.

steps.slogan: Count the states to show that DDF and Virasoro states span the Fock space.
steps.detail: At each level the generating function of the full Fock space is $\prod(1-q^n)^{-26}$. The DDF states give $\prod(1-q^n)^{-24}$, and the Virasoro operators $L_{-n}$ and the second longitudinal family give $\prod(1-q^n)^{-1}$ each. The factors multiply to $\prod(1-q^n)^{-26}$, so these states span.

steps.slogan: Show that a physical state is a DDF state plus a spurious state.
steps.detail: For $D=26$ and intercept $1$, the Kac determinant analysis shows that a physical $\psi$ equals $\psi_\perp+\sum_nL_{-n}\chi_n$ with $\psi_\perp$ in the DDF span. The spurious part is orthogonal to $\psi$, because $\langle\psi|L_{-n}\chi\rangle=\langle L_n\psi|\chi\rangle=0$. It is also orthogonal to $\psi_\perp$, so it has zero norm.

steps.slogan: Read off positivity and the isomorphism with the transverse Fock space.
steps.detail: The norm of $\psi$ equals the norm of $\psi_\perp$, which is nonnegative and equals the transverse oscillator norm. The map $\psi\mapsto\psi_\perp$ is injective modulo null states and surjective because DDF states are physical.

concepts.c:fock-space: It is the state space whose negative-norm states must be shown absent.
concepts.c:virasoro-algebra: Its positive modes define physical states, and its negative modes define spurious ones.

source.ref: P. Goddard and C. B. Thorn, Compatibility of the dual Pomeron with unitarity and the absence of ghosts in the dual resonance model, Physics Letters B 40 (1972), 235-238
source.note: The outline follows the DDF and Kac determinant argument; the decomposition of physical states is cited, not reproved.

statement: Let $I$ be a [subgroup](c:subgroup) of a [direct product](c:direct-product) $G\times H$ whose projections to $G$ and to $H$ are onto. Then there are [normal subgroups](c:normal-subgroup) $M\trianglelefteq G$ and $N\trianglelefteq H$ with $M\times N\le I$, and an isomorphism $e\colon G/M\to H/N$ of [quotient groups](c:quotient-group), such that $I=\{(g,h):e(gM)=hN\}$.

hypotheses.text: The set $I$ is a [subgroup](c:subgroup) of $G\times H$.
The projection $I\to G$ is surjective.
The projection $I\to H$ is surjective.

conclusion: The subgroup $I$ is the preimage of the graph of an isomorphism $G/M\to H/N$ of quotient groups.

formal.difference: The declaration is stated for additive groups, with the image of $I$ in $G/M\times H/N$ equal to the graph of $e$; its multiplicative twin is Subgroup.goursat_surjective. The inclusion $M\times N\le I$ is the separate lemma goursatFst_prod_goursatSnd_le.

proofs.name: Axis subgroups and graph
proofs.slogan: Take $M$ and $N$ as the parts of $I$ on the two axes, then match the cosets of $M$ with the cosets of $N$ through $I$.
proofs.scope: The whole statement, for arbitrary groups. If $I=G\times H$ then $M=G$, $N=H$ and both quotients are trivial.

roles.why: Closure of the [subgroup](c:subgroup) $I$ under products and inverses drives the coset comparison and makes $e$ a homomorphism.
Surjectivity onto $G$ makes $M$ normal and gives every coset of $M$ a partner in $H/N$.
Surjectivity onto $H$ makes $N$ normal and makes $e$ surjective.

steps.slogan: Define $M$ and $N$ as the parts of $I$ lying on the axes.
steps.detail: Put $M=\{g:(g,1)\in I\}$ and $N=\{h:(1,h)\in I\}$. Then $M$ is the image in $G$ of the kernel of the projection $I\to H$, and $N$ is the image in $H$ of the kernel of $I\to G$.

steps.slogan: Show that $M$ and $N$ are [normal subgroups](c:normal-subgroup).
steps.detail: The kernel of $I\to H$ is normal in $I$. A surjective homomorphism maps a normal subgroup onto a normal subgroup, so $M\trianglelefteq G$ because $I\to G$ is onto. The same argument gives $N\trianglelefteq H$.

steps.slogan: Show that equal cosets in $G/M$ match equal cosets in $H/N$.
steps.detail: Let $(g,h),(g',h')\in I$. Then $(g^{-1}g',h^{-1}h')\in I$. If $g^{-1}g'\in M$, then $(g^{-1}g',1)\in I$, and dividing gives $(1,h^{-1}h')\in I$, so $h^{-1}h'\in N$. The converse is symmetric.

steps.slogan: Define $e$ and check that it is an isomorphism of quotient groups.
steps.detail: Send $gM$ to $hN$ for any $(g,h)\in I$; such an $h$ exists because $I\to G$ is onto. The previous step shows that $e$ is well defined and injective. It is a homomorphism because $I$ is a subgroup, and surjective because $I\to H$ is onto. The image of $I$ in $G/M\times H/N$ is the graph of $e$.

steps.slogan: Show that $I$ is the full preimage of the graph of $e$.
steps.detail: Let $e(gM)=hN$. Choose $(g,h')\in I$. Then $h'N=hN$, so $(1,h'^{-1}h)\in I$ and $(g,h)=(g,h')(1,h'^{-1}h)\in I$. Also $M\times N\le I$, since $(g,1)(1,h)=(g,h)$.

concepts.c:subgroup: The set $I$ and the pieces $M$, $N$ are subgroups, and closure drives the argument.
concepts.c:direct-product: The subgroup $I$ sits inside the product, and $M\times N$ lies in it.
concepts.c:normal-subgroup: Normality of $M$ and $N$ lets us form the quotient groups.
concepts.c:quotient-group: The isomorphism $e$ is an isomorphism of these quotients.

source.note: mathlib defines goursatFst and goursatSnd as images of kernels, proves normality with normal_goursatFst and the coset match with mk_goursatFst_eq_iff_mk_goursatSnd_eq, and builds e with MonoidHom.exists_mulEquiv_range_eq_graph.

statement: Let $f\colon X\to Y$ be a generically finite surjective morphism of complex [projective varieties](c:projective-variety) with $X$ smooth. Then the higher [direct images](c:direct-image) of the [canonical sheaf](c:canonical-sheaf) vanish: $R^if_*\omega_X=0$ for all $i>0$.

hypotheses.text: The variety $X$ is smooth, so that $\omega_X$ is the [canonical sheaf](c:canonical-sheaf) of a manifold.
The morphism $f$ is surjective and generically finite, so $\dim X=\dim Y$.
The varieties $X$ and $Y$ are [projective](c:projective-variety) over $\mathbb{C}$.

conclusion: The sheaf $R^if_*\omega_X$ is zero for every $i>0$.

proofs.name: Reduction to Kawamata-Viehweg vanishing
proofs.slogan: Twist by a high power of an ample bundle on $Y$, apply Kawamata-Viehweg vanishing on $X$, and deduce that the higher direct images have no global sections.
proofs.scope: The projective case over $\mathbb{C}$, which contains proper birational morphisms of projective varieties. Grauert and Riemenschneider proved the analytic case for proper holomorphic maps by analytic methods.

roles.why: Smoothness of $X$ lets Kawamata-Viehweg vanishing apply to $\omega_X$ twisted by a nef and big bundle.
Generic finiteness and surjectivity make $f^*A$ big as well as nef.
Projectivity gives an ample bundle $A$ on $Y$ and Serre vanishing and global generation for its powers.

steps.slogan: Pull back an [ample line bundle](c:ample-sheaf) from $Y$ to $X$.
steps.detail: Let $A$ be ample on $Y$. The bundle $f^*A$ is nef because $A$ is ample, and it is big because $f$ is generically finite and surjective: $(f^*A)^n=\deg(f)\,A^n>0$ for $n=\dim X=\dim Y$. Every power $f^*A^m$ is again nef and big.

steps.slogan: Apply Kawamata-Viehweg vanishing to $\omega_X\otimes f^*A^m$.
steps.detail: The theorem applies to $K_X+f^*A^m$ with $f^*A^m$ nef and big on the smooth variety $X$. It gives $H^q(X,\omega_X\otimes f^*A^m)=0$ for all $q>0$ and all $m\ge1$.

steps.slogan: Collapse the Leray spectral sequence for large $m$.
steps.detail: Each $R^qf_*\omega_X$ is a [coherent sheaf](c:coherent-sheaf), and only finitely many are nonzero. By Serre vanishing choose $m$ with $H^p(Y,R^qf_*\omega_X\otimes A^m)=0$ for $p>0$ and all $q$. The Leray spectral sequence and the projection formula then give $H^0(Y,R^qf_*\omega_X\otimes A^m)\cong H^q(X,\omega_X\otimes f^*A^m)$.

steps.slogan: Use global generation to show that the sheaf itself is zero.
steps.detail: The two previous steps give $H^0(Y,R^qf_*\omega_X\otimes A^m)=0$ for $q>0$. Enlarging $m$, the sheaf $R^qf_*\omega_X\otimes A^m$ is generated by global sections, so it is zero. Since $A^m$ is invertible, $R^qf_*\omega_X=0$ for every $q>0$.

concepts.c:canonical-sheaf: It is the sheaf $\omega_X$ whose higher direct images vanish.
concepts.c:direct-image: The theorem says that the higher direct images of $\omega_X$ are zero.
concepts.c:projective-variety: Projectivity gives the ample bundle on $Y$ and Serre vanishing.
concepts.c:ample-sheaf: An ample bundle on $Y$ pulls back to a nef and big bundle on $X$.
concepts.c:coherent-sheaf: Coherence makes Serre vanishing and global generation apply to $R^qf_*\omega_X$.

source.note: The deduction from Kawamata-Viehweg vanishing in R. Lazarsfeld, Positivity in Algebraic Geometry I, section 4.3; the theorem is due to H. Grauert and O. Riemenschneider, Invent. Math. 11 (1970).
